question: A 36-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician’s office with low back pain for the past 5 days. Examination reveals the standing flexion test positive on the right, ASIS superior on the right, PSIS superior on the left, pubic symphysis symmetrical. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Lateralize first: the standing flexion test is positive on the right, so read only right-sided landmarks. Left PSIS superior = right PSIS inferior; with the right ASIS superior, that is a right posterior innominate rotation (ASIS up, PSIS down). Pubic symphysis is symmetrical, so it is not a pubic shear. A superior pubic shear can mimic this pattern but needs a superior pubic tubercle/ramus. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: A 44-year-old man presents to the office with low back pain for the past 6 days. Standing flexion test is positive on the right. The ASIS and PSIS are symmetrical on both sides. The pubic symphysis is superior on the left. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Positive on the right, ASIS/PSIS symmetrical → rules out rotations and up/downslips, leaving flares or pubic shears. Pubic symphysis superior on the left = inferior on the right → right inferior pubic shear. Review note: it is treated like an anterior innominate rotation plus ABduction, so the patient uses hamstrings + adductors (instructor corrected himself; not quadriceps). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 74; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 74

question: A 52-year-old man presents to the clinic with a complaint of back pain for the past 4 days. Structural examination reveals: Standing flexion test positive on the right; Left ASIS is superior; Right PSIS is superior. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Positive on the right. Left ASIS superior = right ASIS inferior; right PSIS superior. ASIS down + PSIS up = anterior innominate rotation. An inferior pubic shear can mimic this, but it requires an inferior pubic tubercle, and an inferior innominate shear would have the PSIS inferior too. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: A 17-year-old woman presents to the office with the complaint of low back pain after playing a soccer game 2 days ago. Reflexes, sensation, and motor strength are normal in the lower extremities bilaterally. Structural exam reveals: Standing flexion test positive on the right; ASIS compression test positive on the right; PSIS inferior on left; ASIS inferior on right. To treat this patient’s somatic dysfunction using a post-isometric muscle energy technique, the activating force is which of the following muscles?
explanation: Positive right; PSIS inferior on the left = superior on the right; ASIS inferior on the right → right anterior innominate rotation. ME setup: flex the hip and knee; the patient pushes the knee into your shoulder (hip extension) using the hamstrings — semimembranosus. Quadriceps/iliopsoas flex the hip and would be used for a posterior rotation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 75; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 75

question: What would the physician expect to find with a right outflare innominate?
A: Narrow sacral sulcus on the right
B: Positive seated flexion test on the right
C: Positive standing flexion test on the left
explanation: Use your hands: an outflare swings the ASIS laterally and the PSIS medially, narrowing the sacral sulcus on that side. The seated flexion test is for sacroiliac (sacral) problems, the standing flexion test would be positive on the right (same side), an outflare gaps rather than compresses the pubic symphysis, and the PSIS is medial, not lateral. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 72; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 72

question: A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician’s office with low back pain of four days duration. The pain is localized to the lumbar and sacroiliac region. It does not radiate. He describes the pain as a moderate ache (5 out of 10).: Structural Exam:; Standing flexion test positive on the right; PSIS superior on the left; ASIS inferior on the left; Medial malleolus superior on the right. Which of the following is most likely the correct diagnosis?
explanation: Positive on the right. PSIS superior on the left = right PSIS inferior; ASIS inferior on the left = right ASIS superior → right posterior innominate rotation. A superior medial malleolus (short leg) on the right fits a posterior rotation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician’s office with low back pain of four days duration. The pain is localized to the lumbar and sacroiliac region. It does not radiate. He describes the pain as a moderate ache (5 out of 10).: Structural Exam:; ASIS compression test positive on the right; PSIS superior on the left; ASIS inferior on the left; Medial malleolus superior on the right. Which of the following is most likely the correct diagnosis?
explanation: Same findings as the prior question but lateralized with the ASIS compression test instead of the standing flexion test — either test lateralizes. Right PSIS inferior + right ASIS superior + short right leg = right posterior innominate rotation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 68; PIAT review transcript.

question: A 24-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of “hip pain” for the past 3 days. He states that he was playing soccer and slipped in the grass. Structural exam findings include a standing flexion test positive on the left, right superior ASIS, left superior PSIS, pubic symphysis is symmetrical, and ASIS to umbilicus equal bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Standing flexion positive on the LEFT, so convert to the left side: right ASIS superior = left ASIS inferior; left PSIS superior. ASIS down + PSIS up on the left = left anterior innominate rotation. Symmetric pubic symphysis and equal ASIS-to-umbilicus distances rule out pubic shear and flares. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: A 36-year-old man presents to the office with low back pain of four days duration. His pain is in the lumbosacral region and does not radiate. He describes the pain as a moderate ache. Standing flexion test is positive on the right. The ASIS and PSIS are symmetrical on both sides. The pubic symphysis is inferior on the right. Which of the following is most likely the correct diagnosis?
explanation: Positive right with symmetrical ASIS and PSIS narrows the choices to flares or pubic shears; the pubic symphysis is inferior on the right → right inferior pubic shear. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 74; PIAT review transcript.

question: When referring to the sacrum, which of the following is the cranial axis?
explanation: The superior transverse axis is the cranial (primary respiratory) axis. The middle transverse axis is the postural axis (sacral flexion/extension), and the inferior transverse axis is where the innominates rotate on the sacrum. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 66; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 66

question: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic with a complaint of back pain of two days duration. Prior to symptom onset, he recalls mis-stepping off a curb, but denies any other trauma. The physician suspects a pelvic somatic dysfunction is the cause of the patient’s chief complaint. The physician notices the following on structural examination: Positive standing flexion test on the right; Right ASIS is inferior; Right PSIS is superior. What is the physician’s diagnosis?
explanation: Right-sided findings read directly: ASIS inferior + PSIS superior = anterior innominate rotation. A shear moves ASIS and PSIS in the same direction; a posterior rotation is the opposite pattern. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic with a complaint of back pain of two days duration. Prior to symptom onset, he recalls mis-stepping off a curb, but denies any other trauma. The physician suspects a pelvic somatic dysfunction is the cause of the patient’s chief complaint. The physician notices the following on structural examination: Positive ASIS compression test on the right; Left ASIS is superior; Left PSIS is inferior. What is the physician’s diagnosis?
explanation: ASIS compression positive on the right. Left ASIS superior = right ASIS inferior; left PSIS inferior = right PSIS superior → right anterior innominate rotation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: A patient fell backward onto the ice and landed on his buttocks. Evaluation reveals a positive standing flexion test on the right, ASIS inferior on the left, PSIS inferior on the left, and SI joint pain on the right. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: A fall onto the buttocks suggests a shear. Positive on the right: left ASIS and PSIS inferior = right ASIS and PSIS both superior — the whole hemipelvis is up → right superior innominate shear (upslip). Note it is an innominate shear, not a pubic shear. ME/HVLA: hip slightly flexed, ABducted ~20° and internally rotated (close-packs the hip), then traction. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 73; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 73

question: A patient has a positive standing flexion test on the right. The seated flexion test is negative. The left ASIS is superior and the left PSIS is inferior. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: The seated flexion test is negative, so this is iliosacral. Positive right standing flexion; left ASIS superior = right ASIS inferior; left PSIS inferior = right PSIS superior → right anterior innominate rotation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: During a structural exam it is noted that a patient has an innominate somatic dysfunction with a left positive standing flexion test. The patient’s left hip and knee are flexed into the “frog leg” position, and the patient is instructed to gently push their knee toward the ceiling. What is the somatic dysfunction being treated?
explanation: Frog-leg = hip flexed and ABducted, which engages the barrier for an ADducted innominate. The patient pushes the knee toward the ceiling, i.e., back toward ADduction, the direction it likes to go (post-isometric). An ADducted innominate is an inflare. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 78; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 78

question: Around which of the sacral axes do the innominates rotate?
explanation: The innominates rotate relative to the sacrum around the inferior transverse axis. Superior = cranial/respiratory; middle = postural (sacral flexion/extension); oblique axes are used in sacral torsions and psoas syndrome. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 66; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 66

question: A 46-year-old man presents to the office with low back pain of three days duration. Evaluation at L4 reveals the spinous process is positioned to the left compared to L5, and symmetry is not restored with lumbar flexion or extension. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this L4 somatic dysfunction?
explanation: L4 spinous process to the left means the body is rotated right (posterior TP on the right). No change with flexion or extension = neutral (type I), so side-bending is opposite rotation: N SL RR. ME/HVLA setup: side-bend right, rotate left; BLT is indirect (take it the way it likes to go). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14

question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the office with low back pain of three days duration. Evaluation reveals L5 has a left anterior transverse process. Upon extension, the transverse processes become more asymmetrical. Which of the following is the most likely somatic dysfunction of L5?
explanation: A left anterior TP means the right TP is posterior → rotated right. It worsens with extension, so it improves with flexion → type II, flexed, rotated and side-bent to the same side: F RR SR. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14

question: Herniation of the L4 intervertebral disc would most likely affect which nerve root?
explanation: X+1 rule: a herniation at the L4 (L4–L5) disc affects the L5 nerve root, because the L4 root has already exited above the disc. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 42; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 42

question: Which of the following would most likely be true regarding a patient with a positive hip drop test on the left?
A: Gluteus medius is weak on the right
B: Thoracolumbar spine has decreased side-bending to the right
C: Thoracolumbar spine has decreased side-bending to the left
D: Gluteus medius is weak on the left
E: Iliopsoas is restricted on the right
explanation: Positive hip drop on the left = the left iliac crest fails to drop 20–25° when the left knee bends, which means the thoracolumbar spine cannot side-bend toward the weight-bearing RIGHT side. Gluteus medius weakness is tested by the Trendelenburg test. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 56; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 56

question: A 52-year-old man presents to the clinic with low back pain for the past week. Structural exam reveals the transverse process of L4 is more anterior on the left. This finding seems to resolve during backward bending. Which of the following is the diagnosis for the L4 somatic dysfunction?
explanation: Left TP anterior = right TP posterior → rotated right. It resolves with backward bending (extension) → type II extended, same-side: E RR SR. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14

question: A counterstrain tender point is found medial to the anterior inferior iliac spine. Which tender point does this represent?
explanation: AL2 is medial to the AIIS. AL1 is medial to the ASIS, AL3 lateral to the AIIS, AL4 inferior to the AIIS, and AL5 on the anterior-superior pubic ramus lateral to the symphysis. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 24; PIAT review transcript.

question: Bamboo spine is associated with which of the following conditions?
explanation: Bamboo spine is the radiographic picture of ankylosing spondylitis, where the vertebrae fuse. In the review the instructor called this an older term that isn't used much anymore. Reference: PIAT exam review (Fotopoulos 11.16.26); PIAT review transcript.

question: A 26-year-old woman presents to the office complaining of back pain for the past three weeks. On physical exam, the physician finds a tender area approximately one inch superior and lateral to the PSIS. Which ligament is most likely affected?
explanation: The iliolumbar ligament is the first ligament to become tender with lumbar postural changes; its tender area is about 1 inch superior and lateral to the PSIS. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 39; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 39

question: Which of the following is a red flag for lumbar pain?
explanation: Red flags: age ≥50, history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, failure to improve with 1 month of therapy, and NO relief with bed rest. The other choices are the reassuring opposites. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 59; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 59

question: Which of the following findings would most likely be associated with a superior pubic shear?
A: Greater distance between the ASIS and umbilicus on the affected side
B: Inferior pubic tubercle on the affected side
C: Superior ASIS on the contralateral side
D: Superior ischial tuberosity on the ipsilateral side
E: Superior pubic ramus on the affected side
explanation: A superior pubic shear has a superior pubic tubercle/ramus on the affected side. It may look like a posterior innominate rotation; a posterior rotation moves the ipsilateral ischial tuberosity DOWN, so a superior ischial tuberosity would be contralateral, not ipsilateral. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 74; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 74

question: A positive seated flexion test is determined by the PSIS moving in which of the following directions?
explanation: Positive seated (and standing) flexion test = the PSIS on that side moves more cephalad at the end of forward bending, because the restricted SI joint carries it up. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 69; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 69

question: What does a positive seated flexion test indicate?
explanation: Seated flexion removes the innominates (legs) from the picture, so a positive test points to a sacroiliac (sacrum-on-ilium) problem. The standing flexion test points to an iliosacral problem. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 69; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 69

question: Herniation of the L3 intervertebral disc would most likely affect which nerve root?
explanation: X+1 rule: L3 disc herniation affects the L4 nerve root. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 42; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 42

question: A positive seated flexion test is determined by the PSIS moving in which of the following directions?
explanation: Positive seated flexion test = PSIS moves superiorly (cephalad) on the restricted side at end range. Exams may say 'cephalad', 'superiorly', or 'moves furthest'. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 69; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 69

question: What does a positive standing flexion test indicate?
explanation: The standing flexion test is the gold-standard test for iliosacral (ilium-on-sacrum) somatic dysfunction; the seated flexion test is for sacroiliac. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 67; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 67

question: A positive standing flexion test is determined by the PSIS moving in which of the following directions?
explanation: Positive standing flexion test = PSIS moves superiorly (more cephalad) on the restricted side at end range of forward bending. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 67; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 67

question: Herniation of the L4 intervertebral disc would most likely affect which nerve root?
explanation: X+1 rule: L4 disc → L5 nerve root. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 42; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 42

question: A positive standing flexion test is determined by the PSIS moving in which of the following directions?
explanation: Positive standing flexion test = PSIS moves more cephalad on the restricted side at end range. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 67; PIAT review transcript.

question: Gluteus medius weakness would indicate which of the following tests as positive?
explanation: The Trendelenburg test assesses gluteus medius strength: standing on one leg, the pelvis drops toward the lifted side when the stance-side gluteus medius is weak. Hip drop tests lumbar side-bending, Ober tests TFL/IT band, Thomas tests psoas, SLR tests disc/sciatic. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 55; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 55

question: A 24-year-old man presents to the office with the complaint of low back pain for the past 2 days. The ASIS compression test is positive on the left. The ASIS is superior on the right, the PSIS is superior on the left, and the pubic symphysis is level. The initial set up for a muscle energy technique related to this patient’s presentation would be which of the following?
explanation: ASIS compression positive on the left. Right ASIS superior = left ASIS inferior; left PSIS superior → left anterior innominate rotation. ME setup: FLEX the left hip (and knee) to rotate the innominate posteriorly; the patient then extends with the hamstrings. Extending the hip is the setup for a posterior rotation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 75; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 75

question: A 34-year-old woman presents to the office with the complaint of low back pain for the past 4 days. L5 has a posterior transverse process on the right in both neutral and extended position. What is the most likely lumbar somatic dysfunction?
explanation: Posterior right TP = rotated right. It stays asymmetric in neutral and extension, so it must improve in flexion → F RR SR (type II, same-side). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14

question: A 34-year-old woman presents to the office with the complaint of low back pain for the past 4 days. L5 has a posterior transverse process on the right in both neutral and extended position. What is the initial set up for a muscle energy technique?
explanation: The dysfunction is F RR SR, so the direct (ME) setup goes to the barrier in all three planes: extended, rotated left, side-bent left. Post-isometric: the patient pushes toward F RR SR while the physician holds an unyielding counterforce toward E RL SL. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14; PIAT review transcript.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14

question: A 46-year-old man presents to the office with low back pain and left hip pain for the past 2 days after playing golf. Structural exam reveals: Positive ASIS compression test on the right; ASIS caudad and slightly medial on the right; PSIS cephalad and slightly lateral on the right; Pubic symphysis is level. To treat this patient’s somatic dysfunction using a joint mobilization muscle energy technique, in which of the following directions should the patient be instructed push their hip?
explanation: ASIS caudad and slightly medial with PSIS cephalad and slightly lateral is board wording for an anterior innominate rotation (the innominate rotates down and slightly in). Joint-mobilization ME: flex the hip to the barrier; the patient pushes into EXTENSION (hamstrings). Don't confuse the patient's push with the setup. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71; PIAT review transcript.

question: A 58-year-old man in the clinic for low back OMT suddenly develops crushing substernal chest pain and shortness of breath. Thoracic paraspinal tissue texture changes are palpable at T2–T4. What is the most appropriate next step?
A: Stop and stabilize the patient; OMT is deferred
B: Treat the T2–T4 somatic dysfunction with HVLA
C: Treat with counterstrain because it is indirect and gentle
D: Apply muscle energy to the upper thoracic spine
E: Perform rib raising to reduce sympathetic tone
explanation: For ANY disease state the patient must be STABLE before OMT; new chest pain or shortness of breath is not a time for OMT. The tissue changes are likely a viscerosomatic reflex, but finding them does not justify treating an unstable patient, regardless of how gentle the technique is. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 2.

question: Somatic dysfunction can occur at sympathetic, parasympathetic, or purely somatic levels. At which levels can a facilitated segment occur?
E: Any spinal level, including the sacrum
explanation: Facilitated segments ONLY occur at sympathetic levels. Viscerosomatic reflexes can occur at both sympathetic and parasympathetic levels, and somatic dysfunction can occur anywhere. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 2.

question: A 35-year-old man with a ureteral stone has right lower quadrant/flank pain. When he holds his left knee to his chest, his right thigh will not lie flat on the table. What best explains this finding?
A: Direct irritation of the psoas by the overlying ureter
B: Iliolumbar ligament strain from postural change
C: Right piriformis spasm compressing the sciatic nerve
E: Weakness of the right gluteus medius
explanation: This is a positive Thomas test (psoas hypertonicity). Structures overlying a muscle can irritate it directly: a ureteral stone (or appendicitis) can make the psoas hypertonic. Gluteus medius weakness = Trendelenburg; TFL tightness = Ober. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 3.

question: During motion testing, the T11–L2 group translates easily to the left but resists translation to the right. What is the side-bending component of this group?
explanation: Translation to the left induces right side-bending. Since the group moves freely to the left (and is restricted to the right), it likes to side-bend right. Quick rule from review: the direction of restricted translation = the side of side-bending. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 15.

question: A 31-year-old man with a history of IV drug use has 3 weeks of constant, worsening low back pain, low-grade fevers, and point tenderness over L3. Which condition should be considered before treating with OMT?
D: Type II somatic dysfunction of L3
explanation: Osteomyelitis may occur after an invasive orthopedic procedure or IV drug use. Fever plus focal spinal tenderness in this setting is a disease state to rule out, not a somatic dysfunction to treat. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 3.

question: A 22-year-old sprinter has chronically tight hamstrings. Which innominate somatic dysfunction is this most likely to cause?
explanation: Hamstrings attach to the ischial tuberosity; when tight they pull it down and rotate the innominate posteriorly. Tight quadriceps (rectus femoris on the AIIS) cause an anterior innominate rotation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 3.

question: A patient has an anatomic short right leg with a compensated lumbar curve. Which lumbar pattern is expected?
explanation: The lumbar spine side-bends toward the LONG leg (left) and rotates toward the SHORT leg (right), type I-like mechanics. The hip drop test must be normal for this compensation to occur. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 3.

question: A 14-year-old has a reversible dextroscoliosis from T4 to T6. How are these vertebrae described?
explanation: Reversible = no sagittal component = Fryette type I. Dextroscoliosis is convex right, so the group side-bends into the concavity (left) and rotates toward the convexity (right): N SL RR. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 4.

question: A patient has a group curve from L1 to L5 with a lateral convexity to the left. If you treat the group, which segment do you target and what is its side-bending component?
explanation: A left lateral convexity means the vertebrae are side-bent right (concavity on the right). For a group dysfunction, treat the apex: L1–L5 → L3 (L1–L3 → L2). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 4.

question: Paraspinal tissue at T6 feels cool, dry, smooth, and ropy, with decreased tone and restricted motion. Which additional feature is most consistent with this type of somatic dysfunction?
C: Recent onset with sharp localized pain
D: Increased muscle spindle firing with spasm
E: Somatovisceral effects are more often present
explanation: Cool, dry, ropy, fibrotic tissue with restricted ROM is CHRONIC ("old is cold, hot is not"). Chronic dysfunction more often has somatovisceral effects. The other choices describe acute dysfunction. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 6.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 6

question: Where do somatic and visceral afferent fibers synapse to produce a viscerosomatic reflex?
A: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
E: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord
explanation: Somatic and visceral afferents converge in the dorsal horn, giving a viscerosomatic reflex. Postganglionic sympathetic fibers then produce the tissue texture changes (hypertonicity, moisture, erythema). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 6.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 6

question: A patient with a gastric ulcer has tissue texture changes in the mid-thoracic paraspinal muscles. Which osteopathic principle does this best illustrate?
B: Rational treatment is based on the other principles
C: Somatic dysfunction is named for the way it likes to go
D: Structure and function are reciprocally interrelated
E: The body is capable of self-regulation and self-healing
explanation: The study guide's example for Principle 1 (the body is a unit) is a gastric ulcer causing thoracic tissue texture changes. A healed fracture illustrates Principle 2 (self-healing). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 7.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 7

question: A 20-year-old has a swollen, edematous ankle after an inversion sprain. Which osteopathic model would most directly guide treatment of the swelling?
explanation: Swelling is a fluid problem; the respiratory/circulatory model emphasizes circulatory and lymphatic flow and uses lymphatic techniques. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 8.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 8

question: What is the orientation of the lumbar superior facets?
explanation: Lumbar superior facets face Backward and Medial (BM, sometimes BUM). Thoracic superior facets are BUL; cervical are BUM. Inferior lumbar facets face anterior and lateral (AL/AIL). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 10.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 10

question: A group of vertebrae in a neutral spine is side-bent left. According to Fryette's first principle, how do they rotate?
explanation: Fryette I: neutral, group of vertebrae, side-bending precedes rotation, and they occur to opposite sides. Side-bending is toward the concavity, rotation is toward the convexity. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 11.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 11

question: Which statement correctly describes Fryette's second principle?
A: Side-bending and rotation occur to the same side in a neutral group curve
B: Rotation and side-bending occur to opposite sides in a single extended segment
C: Rotation precedes side-bending to the same side in a single flexed or extended segment
D: Motion in one plane has no effect on the other planes
E: Side-bending precedes rotation to the opposite side in a group of vertebrae
explanation: Fryette II: non-neutral (sagittal component present), typically a single vertebra, rotation precedes side-bending, both to the same side, rotation into the concavity. Often traumatic. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 12.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 12

question: You palpate the tip of the T8 spinous process. Using the rule of 3's, which transverse processes lie in the same horizontal plane?
explanation: T7–T9 spinous processes project moderately downward, so the tip lies in the plane of the transverse processes of the vertebra BELOW (T9). T4–T6 are halfway; T1–T3 are the same level. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 17.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 17

question: A technique places the joint in its position of ease, adds a compressive force, then carries the joint through the restrictive barrier while keeping the compression. Which technique is this?
explanation: Still technique starts indirect (ease + compression/traction) and ends direct (to and through the barrier). FPR and counterstrain stay in ease (indirect); muscle energy is direct throughout. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 26.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 26

question: In facilitated positional release, after flattening the curve and adding compression, how long is the position of ease held?
A: Until the tissue softens, usually 2 minutes
C: Repeated 3–5 times for 3–5 seconds against resistance
explanation: FPR: neutral (flatten the curve), compression (or traction), place into ease for 3–5 seconds, return to neutral. Counterstrain is held for 90 seconds; 3–5 repetitions against resistance describes muscle energy. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 25.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 25

question: During counterstrain for a lumbar tender point, the patient rated the tenderness as 10 before treatment. After a 90-second hold and slow return to neutral, which rating indicates an adequate response?
explanation: After counterstrain the tender point should be reduced to 3 or less out of 10. Hold 90 seconds for all points (including ribs), monitor continuously without pressing, and return slowly. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 23.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 23

question: During muscle energy for an extended lumbar segment, the physician positions the segment at the restrictive barrier and asks the patient to gently push further INTO the barrier against resistance. Which type of muscle energy is this?
explanation: Patient pushes toward/into the barrier = reciprocal inhibition. Patient pushes away from the barrier (the way the dysfunction likes to go) = post-isometric relaxation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 28.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 28

question: Counterstrain and facilitated positional release are both thought to work mainly by resetting which structure?
explanation: Counterstrain and FPR act on muscle spindles (Ia/II afferents and gamma gain). Muscle energy loads tension on Golgi tendon organs to produce relaxation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 25.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 25

question: A patient with an acute myocardial infarction begins vomiting. Which type of reflex is this?
explanation: Visceral stimulus → visceral response = viscerovisceral (MI and vomiting). Gallbladder disease affecting musculature = viscerosomatic; asthma triggered by thoracic treatment = somatovisceral; innominate causing rib dysfunction = somatosomatic. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 29.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 29

question: A patient passes a stone lodged in the LOWER ureter. At which spinal levels would viscerosomatic tissue texture changes most likely be found?
explanation: Upper ureters: T10–T11. Lower ureters: T12–L1. Bladder: T12–L2. S2–S4 is the parasympathetic supply to the lower ureter, not a sympathetic level. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 30.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 30

question: Which nerve supply provides the parasympathetic innervation to the distal ureter and bladder?
explanation: Parasympathetics: vagus to structures down to the splenic flexure and the proximal ureter; S2–S4 to the distal ureter, bladder, descending/sigmoid colon, rectum and reproductive organs. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 31.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 31

question: A patient with acute appendicitis shows viscerosomatic changes. Through which splanchnic nerve and ganglion does the appendix receive its sympathetic supply?
A: Least splanchnic nerve to the inferior mesenteric ganglion
B: Greater splanchnic nerve to the celiac ganglion
C: Pelvic splanchnic nerves to the inferior hypogastric plexus
D: Lumbar splanchnic nerves to the inferior mesenteric ganglion
E: Lesser splanchnic nerve to the superior mesenteric ganglion
explanation: Lesser splanchnic (T10–T11) synapses in the superior mesenteric ganglion and supplies the small intestine and right colon, including the appendix. Greater splanchnic (T5–T9) → celiac; least/lumbar (T12–L2) → inferior mesenteric. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 34.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 34

question: A Chapman reflex point is found in the 7th intercostal space next to the sternum on the RIGHT. Which organ does it represent?
explanation: Right 7th IC space = pancreas (think glucose, amylase, lipase); left 7th = spleen. Right 5th = liver, right 6th = liver/gallbladder. Appendix = tip of the right 12th rib. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 37.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 37

question: A patient taking daily NSAIDs has epigastric pain. Which anterior Chapman point would most likely be tender?
A: Left 5th intercostal space near the sternum
B: Right 7th intercostal space near the sternum
C: Right 5th intercostal space near the sternum
E: Left 6th intercostal space near the sternum
explanation: Left 5th IC space = stomach acid (gastritis, NSAID/steroid use). Left 6th = stomach peristalsis (emptying); right 5th = liver; right 7th = pancreas. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 37.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 37

question: Which spinal levels supply sympathetic innervation to the lower extremity vasculature?
A: There is parasympathetic but no sympathetic supply
explanation: Upper extremity vasculature: T2–T8. Lower extremity: T11–L2. There is NO parasympathetic supply to the upper or lower extremities. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 35.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 35

question: Before performing pedal pumps on a patient with lower extremity edema, which area must be treated first?
explanation: The thoracic inlet must be opened before ANY lymphatic treatment, because that is where lymph returns to the venous system. Open the transition zones (inlet, thoracoabdominal diaphragm, pelvic diaphragm) to let fluid move. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 100.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 100

question: Which structure is a component of the thoracic inlet that should be checked for somatic dysfunction before lymphatic treatment?
explanation: Thoracic inlet components include the supraclavicular space and the 1st rib (with T1, the clavicles, and the anterior/middle scalenes that attach to rib 1). Fixing 1st rib dysfunction is a listed treatment. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 100.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 100

question: Which is a stated goal of lymphatic treatment?
A: Increase sympathetic tone to the extremities
explanation: Lymphatic goals: remove barriers, promote lymphatic flow (increase reabsorption, increase circulation/respiration, decrease interstitial proteins), drain toxins, assist regeneration, stimulate immune function, diminish sympathetic tone, retain treatment gains. Expect questions that flip one of these. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 101.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 101

question: A 40-year-old has a long-standing 8 mm anatomic short right leg with low back pain. What final heel-lift height is appropriate under the right heel?
explanation: For a chronic discrepancy, lift ½–¾ of the measured difference: 8 mm → 4–6 mm. Only 5 mm fits. The full amount is used only for a recent, sudden cause (hip fracture, prosthesis). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 97.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 97

question: Two months after a hip replacement, a patient has a new 10 mm leg length discrepancy. What final heel-lift height is appropriate?
explanation: A recent, sudden cause (hip fracture, prosthesis) is lifted the FULL amount. Chronic discrepancies get ½–¾ (here 5–7.5 mm). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 97.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 97

question: An 82-year-old woman with osteoporosis needs a heel lift. How should the lift be started and advanced?
A: Apply the full calculated amount at once
B: Start at 1/4 inch and increase by 1/8 inch every week
C: Start at 1/16 inch and increase by 1/16 inch every two weeks
D: Start at 1/16 inch and increase by 1/8 inch every week
E: Start at 1/8 inch and increase by 1/8 inch every two weeks
explanation: Fragile patients (elderly, arthritic, osteoporotic, acute pain) start at 1/16 inch and increase 1/16 inch every two weeks. Flexible patients start at 1/8 inch and increase 1/8 inch every two weeks. Max 1/4 inch inside the shoe; max heel lift 1/2 inch. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 97.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 97

question: When is heel lift treatment considered clinically complete?
A: When the leg lengths measure equal on X-ray
C: When the hip drop test becomes positive
E: When the full measured discrepancy has been lifted
explanation: Heel lift treatment is complete when the patient's painful symptoms are reduced. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 98.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Recall
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 98

question: In short leg syndrome, which innominate finding is expected on the side of the SHORT leg?
explanation: Short leg syndrome: anterior innominate on the short-leg side, posterior innominate on the long-leg side; the L-spine side-bends away from and rotates toward the short leg; the lumbosacral angle increases; the iliolumbar ligaments are stressed first. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 99.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 99

question: A 13-year-old has a right thoracic rib hump. When she side-bends toward the hump, it largely disappears. What is the first conclusion?
B: This is a junctional cervicothoracic curve
C: This is a double major curve
E: This is a structural scoliosis needing bracing
explanation: The first step in scoliosis is to evaluate reversibility. If side-bending toward the rib hump reduces it, the curve is functional; a structural curve stays fixed with position changes (give home exercises). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 96.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 96

question: Months after a left-hemisphere stroke, a patient walks by swinging the right leg outward in an arc with the right arm held flexed. Which gait is this?
explanation: Hemiplegic gait = unilateral hip flexion with circumduction from weak extensors, with ipsilateral upper-extremity flexion; common post-stroke. Spastic/scissor gait is bilateral (e.g., cerebral palsy). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 93.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 93

question: A patient lifts the right foot unusually high with each step so the toes clear the ground. Which nerve root is most likely involved?
explanation: This is steppage (foot drop) gait from weak dorsiflexion, seen in L5 and fibular neuropathies. L5 supplies the extensor hallucis longus and dorsiflexors. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 93.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Application
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 93

question: A patient with right knee pain walks with a limp. Which change in the right leg's gait cycle is expected?
explanation: Antalgic gait avoids pain by shortening the stance phase on the painful side relative to swing. Wide base = ataxic; shuffling = festinating (Parkinson's); circumduction = hemiplegic. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 92.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 92

question: Which finding would NOT be classified as a somatic dysfunction?
A: A rotated L3 with tenderness and restricted motion
E: A healing compression fracture of L1
explanation: Not all somatic lesions are somatic dysfunction: fractures, sprains, degenerative and inflammatory processes are not. Somatic dysfunction is diagnosed by TART and named for the way it likes to go. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 5.
section: Osteopathic Concepts & Techniques | Exam Style | Understanding
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 5

question: An X-ray shows that S1 is not fused to the rest of the sacrum and behaves like a sixth lumbar vertebra. What is this called?
explanation: Lumbarization = S1 acts like a 6th lumbar vertebra (S2 acts like the sacral base). Sacralization = L5 is fused to the sacrum and functions as the sacral base. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 40.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 40

question: Why do lumbar disc herniations most commonly occur posterolaterally?
A: The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow
B: The anterior longitudinal ligament is weak
C: The nucleus pulposus is thickest anteriorly
D: The facets are oriented in the coronal plane
E: The iliolumbar ligament pulls the disc laterally
explanation: Posterolateral herniation is most common because the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and does not cover the posterolateral annulus. Most common levels: L4–L5 and L5–S1. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 41.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 41

question: A 45-year-old has low back pain radiating down the leg, weakness of great-toe extension, numbness over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, and normal reflexes. Herniation of which disc is most likely?
explanation: These are L5 root findings (EHL weakness, lateral leg/dorsum sensory loss, no reflex to test). By the X+1 rule, the L4–L5 disc compresses the L5 root. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 46.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 46

question: A patient cannot walk on her toes, has numbness of the lateral malleolus and lateral foot, and a diminished Achilles reflex. Which nerve root is affected?
explanation: S1: Achilles reflex, plantarflexion/eversion (gastrocnemius, peroneals) — can't toe-walk — and sensation of the lateral malleolus and lateral foot. Usually from an L5–S1 herniation. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 46.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 46

question: A patient has a diminished patellar reflex, weak foot inversion, and decreased sensation over the medial leg. Which disc herniation best explains this?
explanation: L4 root: patellar reflex, anterior tibialis (inversion)/quads, medial leg and foot sensation. X+1 rule: the L3–L4 disc affects the L4 root. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 46.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 46

question: During a straight leg raise, the patient's radicular pain begins at 50° of hip flexion. What does this range suggest?
A: Joint (hip/SI) pain rather than nerve pain
C: Only slight tension on the sciatic nerve
E: Maximal involvement of the sciatic nerve
explanation: SLR: 0–35° = some sciatic tension; 35–70° = maximal sciatic involvement; >70° = most likely joint pain. A positive SLR does not by itself prove a herniated disc. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 49.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 49

question: After a positive straight leg raise, the leg is lowered until pain-free and the ankle is dorsiflexed, which reproduces the radicular pain. What does this indicate?
explanation: Bragard test: lower the leg until pain-free, then dorsiflex the ankle to tension the dural sheath; reproducing symptoms = radiculopathy. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 51.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 51

question: Stroking the sole of a patient's foot causes the great toe to extend and the other toes to fan. What does this indicate?
explanation: A positive Babinski (upgoing toe) indicates upper motor neuron pathology. The normal response is a downgoing plantar reflex (not called a 'negative Babinski'). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 48.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 48

question: With the patient's hip in flexion, abduction, external rotation, and then extension (figure-4), the patient reports pain in the posterior pelvis. What is the most likely source?
explanation: FABERE (Patrick) test assesses SI joint vs hip: posterior pain = SI joint; anterior (groin) pain = hip. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 53.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 53

question: With the patient side-lying, knee flexed and hip extended, the thigh cannot drop (adduct) past midline. Which structure is tight?
explanation: Ober's test assesses contracture/tightness of the iliotibial band or tensor fascia latae; positive if the thigh cannot adduct past midline. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 54.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 54

question: A patient asks for opioids for leg weakness. When he 'tries' to lift his right leg off the table, you feel no downward pressure from his left heel in your hand. What does this suggest?
explanation: Hoover test: when a patient genuinely tries to raise one leg, the opposite heel presses down. Absent counter-pressure suggests the patient is not giving real effort (malingering/secondary gain). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 58.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 58

question: A patient stands on her RIGHT leg and lifts the left foot; her left hip drops. Which muscle is weak, and what exercise is indicated?
A: Right gluteus medius; hip adduction exercises
B: Left gluteus medius; hip abduction exercises
D: Right piriformis; hip external rotation exercises
E: Right gluteus medius; hip abduction exercises
explanation: Positive Trendelenburg: the stance-side gluteus medius cannot keep the pelvis level, so the opposite hip drops. Weak right gluteus medius → strengthen with abduction exercises (assuming no nerve damage). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 55.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 55

question: When a patient bends the RIGHT knee (heel on the floor), the right iliac crest drops only 5° and the lumbar curve stays flat. What does this mean?
C: Decreased lumbar side-bending to the left
E: Decreased lumbar side-bending to the right
explanation: Positive hip drop on the right: the crest does not drop 20–25°, so the lumbar spine cannot side-bend toward the weight-bearing (left) side — the side opposite the positive test. Gluteus medius is the Trendelenburg test. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 56.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 56

question: Which finding is a red flag in a patient presenting with low back pain?
A: Pain that improves with bed rest
B: Pain localized to the paraspinal muscles
explanation: Lumbar red flags: age ≥50, previous cancer, unexplained weight loss, failure to improve with 1 month of therapy, NO relief with bed rest. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 59.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 59

question: L3 has a posterior transverse process on the left that becomes symmetric when the patient extends. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Posterior left TP = rotated left. Improves with extension = extended type II, same-side: E RL SL. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14

question: An L5 transverse process on the left is SUPERIOR compared to the right, and it moves inferiorly (becomes symmetric) as the patient flexes. What is the side-bending component, and is the segment flexed or extended?
explanation: A superior/inferior TP describes the side-bending component: the left TP is up because the segment is side-bent RIGHT. It improves with flexion → flexed. (A posterior TP describes rotation.) Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 14

question: L2 is N SL RR. For seated post-isometric muscle energy, after localizing to neutral, where should the patient be positioned before the isometric contraction?
explanation: Muscle energy is direct: engage the barrier. For N SL RR, take it to the right side-bending and left rotation barriers. The patient then turns or pulls the right shoulder back (toward the way it likes to go) against an unyielding counterforce. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 61.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 61

question: When setting up seated muscle energy for a TYPE II (extension) lumbar dysfunction, how should the physician's arm pass relative to the patient's arm in the osteopathic salute position?
B: Through the patient's elbows from below
explanation: Type I (neutral) → physician's arm goes UNDER; type II → OVER. The textbook picture for type II was wrong — it should show the arm over. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 63.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 63

question: L4 is N SL RR. Using balanced ligamentous tension, how is the segment positioned?
C: Directly to the restrictive barrier in all planes
explanation: BLT is indirect: take the dysfunction the way it likes to go (exaggerate it) — side-bent left, rotated right. HVLA and muscle energy are direct (side-bend right, rotate left). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 18.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 18

question: A patient with chronic postural strain has pain referred to the groin, SI region and lateral thigh, with tenderness about 1 inch superior and lateral to the PSIS. The ligament involved attaches the iliac crest to which structures?
A: The inferior lateral angle of the sacrum
D: Transverse processes of L4 and L5
E: Spinous processes of L4 and L5
explanation: The iliolumbar ligament runs from the iliac crest to the L4 and L5 transverse processes, stabilizes the lumbosacral junction, refers pain to the groin/SI/lateral thigh, and is the first ligament to become tender with lumbar postural changes. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 39.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 39

question: A patient has a tender point on the anterior-superior aspect of the left pubic ramus, lateral to the symphysis. Which counterstrain point is this, and where does the physician stand?
explanation: AL5 is on the anterior-superior pubic ramus lateral to the symphysis (F SA RA). The physician stands on the SAME side for AL1 and AL5 and the OPPOSITE side for AL2–AL4. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 24.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 24

question: A tender point is found medial to the right ASIS. Which counterstrain acronym describes the treatment position?
explanation: Medial to the ASIS = AL1: Flex, Side-bend Toward, Rotate Away (F ST RA). AL2–4 = F SA RT; AL5 = F SA RA. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 24.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 24

question: A 50-year-old spent the weekend weeding and now stands flexed at the waist, leaning to the RIGHT, with a positive right Thomas test. What is the key somatic dysfunction that perpetuates this syndrome?
A: Type II at L1/L2: flexed, rotated left, side-bent left
B: Type II at L1/L2: flexed, rotated right, side-bent right
C: Type I at L1–L5: neutral, side-bent left, rotated right
D: Type I at L3–L5: neutral, side-bent right, rotated left
E: Type II at L5: extended, rotated left, side-bent left
explanation: Psoas syndrome is driven by a non-neutral (type II) L1 or L2 dysfunction, flexed, side-bent and rotated toward the hypertonic psoas (here right). L3–L5 then follow type I mechanics. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 88.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 88

question: A patient has LEFT psoas syndrome. Which findings are expected on the contralateral side?
A: Pelvic shift right with right piriformis spasm and right sciatic irritation
B: Pelvic shift left with left piriformis spasm and left sciatic irritation
C: Pelvic shift left with right piriformis spasm and right sciatic irritation
D: No pelvic shift; bilateral piriformis spasm
E: Pelvic shift right with left piriformis spasm and right sciatic irritation
explanation: Left psoas syndrome: lumbar spine side-bends left, the sacrum is on the LEFT oblique axis, the pelvis shifts RIGHT, straining the RIGHT piriformis, which irritates the RIGHT sciatic nerve (gluteal/posterior thigh pain usually not past the knee). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 89.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 89

question: Where is the psoas major counterstrain tender point located?
A: Two-thirds of the distance from the ASIS to midline
C: One inch superior and lateral to the PSIS
E: At the tip of the right 12th rib
explanation: Psoas tender point: ⅔ of the distance from the ASIS to the midline (it may also be found at psoas minor/iliacus, and a contralateral piriformis point). Medial to the ASIS is AL1. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 86.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 86

question: Before diagnosing psoas syndrome in a patient with a hypertonic left psoas, which condition should be ruled out?
explanation: Organic causes of psoas spasm must be ruled out: hip bursitis/arthritis, appendicitis, diverticulosis, ureteral calculi, prostatitis, colon cancer, salpingitis, psoas abscess — by viscerosomatic reflex or direct irritation of the psoas fascia. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 85.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 85

question: During the standing flexion test, what does the physician monitor, and what defines the positive side?
B: Inferior PSIS; side moving more cephalad
explanation: The physician monitors the inferior aspect of the PSIS; the positive side is the one whose PSIS travels more cephalad at the end of forward bending. It is the gold-standard test for iliosacral dysfunction. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 67.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 67

question: How is the ASIS compression test performed and interpreted?
A: Downward pressure on the iliac crests; the lower side is positive
B: Anterior pressure on the PSIS; the side that moves more is positive
C: Posterior-medial pressure on one ASIS toward the SI joint; the restricted side is positive
D: Posterior pressure on the pubic symphysis; the tender side is positive
E: Lateral pressure on both ASISs; the painful side is positive
explanation: Stabilize one ASIS and apply posterior-medial pressure on the other, aiming toward the SI joint; repeat on the other side. The restricted side is the positive (lateralizing) side. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 68.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 68

question: Standing flexion test positive on the left. The left ASIS is closer to the umbilicus and more medial than the right; ASIS and PSIS heights are equal; the left sacral sulcus is wide. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Inflare (ADducted): ASIS medial with decreased ASIS–umbilicus distance, PSIS lateral, WIDE sacral sulcus. Outflare is the reverse (ASIS lateral, narrow sulcus). Equal heights rule out rotations and shears. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 72.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 72

question: After stepping off a curb, a patient has a positive right standing flexion test. On the right, the ASIS, PSIS, iliac crest, pubic tubercle, and ischial tuberosity are all inferior, and the medial malleolus is inferior. Which additional finding is expected on the right?
explanation: All landmarks inferior = inferior innominate shear (downslip). The ischial tuberosity is pulled away from the ILA, so the sacrotuberous ligament is TIGHT. In an upslip it is lax. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 73.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 73

question: A patient has a right anterior innominate rotation. Which additional right-sided finding is expected?
A: Deep sacral sulcus and superior ASIS
B: Superior iliac crest and superior pubic tubercle
C: Superior ischial tuberosity and inferior medial malleolus (long leg)
D: Inferior ischial tuberosity and superior medial malleolus (short leg)
E: Lateral ASIS and narrow sacral sulcus
explanation: Anterior rotation: ASIS inferior, PSIS superior, superior ischial tuberosity, SHALLOW sulcus, equal crest heights, medial malleolus inferior (long leg). Posterior rotation has the opposite (inferior ischial tuberosity, deep sulcus, short leg). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: Which pair of findings correctly matches the sacral sulcus to the innominate dysfunction on the same side?
explanation: With the sacrum fixed: posterior rotation pushes the PSIS back → DEEP sulcus; anterior rotation → SHALLOW; inflare → WIDE; outflare → NARROW. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 71

question: A patient has a right innominate outflare. For muscle energy, the right hip and knee are flexed. How is the barrier engaged, and what does the patient do?
A: Apply leg traction; patient pulls the hip cephalad
B: ABduct the knee into frog-leg; patient ADducts against resistance
C: Flex the hip further; patient extends against resistance
D: Extend the hip off the table; patient flexes against resistance
E: ADduct the knee across midline; patient ABducts against resistance
explanation: Outflare (ABducted) ME: flex the hip and knee, ADduct the knee across midline to the barrier while applying lateral force to the medial PSIS; the patient ABducts. Frog-leg with the patient ADducting is the inflare treatment. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 79.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 79

question: A patient with a left posterior innominate rotation is treated PRONE. The physician extends the left hip to the barrier. What does the patient do, and which muscle group is activated?
A: Lifts the leg toward the ceiling (hip extension) with the hamstrings
B: ADducts the hip with the adductors
C: Pulls the knee toward the table (hip flexion) with the hamstrings
D: Pulls the leg toward the table (hip flexion) with the quadriceps
E: Pushes the leg caudad with the gluteus maximus
explanation: Posterior rotation is treated by extending the hip (anterior rotation of the innominate), supine with the leg off the table or prone. Either way the patient flexes the hip — prone, by pulling the leg toward the table — using the quadriceps (rectus femoris). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 77.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 77

question: A patient has a right superior pubic shear. The physician lets the right leg hang off the table, ABducts it, and pushes it into extension. Which combination of muscle actions does the patient use against resistance?
explanation: Superior pubic shear = posterior rotation setup + ABduction to gap the symphysis. The patient pushes the knee toward the ceiling — flexion (quadriceps/rectus femoris) and adduction (adductors). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 80.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 80

question: A patient has a left inferior pubic shear. The physician flexes and ABducts the left hip with the knee against the chest. Which muscle groups does the patient use against resistance?
explanation: Inferior pubic shear = anterior rotation setup (flex the hip) + ABduction. The patient pushes the knee into the chest — extension (hamstrings) and adduction (adductors). The adductors close the gap; the hamstrings bring the pubis up. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 81.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 81

question: When treating a right upslip with muscle energy or HVLA, the leg is internally rotated, slightly flexed and ABducted about 20° before traction. Why is the hip internally rotated?
C: To close-pack the femoral head in the acetabulum
D: To engage the inferior transverse axis
explanation: Internal rotation close-packs (locks) the femoral head in the acetabulum so that traction is transmitted to the innominate. The patient then pulls the hip cephalad against resistance; HVLA uses the same setup with a tug. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 82.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 82

question: Standing flexion test positive on the left. The left pubic tubercle is superior, the left inguinal ligament is tense and tender, and the left ASIS is slightly superior with the PSIS slightly inferior. Which dysfunction is present?
explanation: A superior pubic shear may look like a posteriorly rotated innominate (ASIS up, PSIS down), but the superior pubic tubercle and a tense ipsilateral inguinal ligament identify the pubic shear. An upslip would raise the PSIS too. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 74.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 74

question: Which pair of terms describes the SAME innominate dysfunction?
C: Anterior rotation and inferior innominate shear
explanation: Upslip = superior innominate shear; downslip = inferior innominate shear; outflare = ABducted; inflare = ADducted. Pubic shears are separate dysfunctions at the symphysis. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 70.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 70

question: Around which sacral axis does the sacral base flex and extend during posture changes?
explanation: Middle transverse = postural axis (sacral flexion/extension). Superior transverse = cranial/respiratory. Inferior transverse = innominate rotation. Oblique axes are engaged in torsions (e.g., psoas syndrome). Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 66.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 66

question: For a right anterior innominate rotation treated with post-isometric muscle energy, the patient's leg rests on the physician's shoulder. What does the physician do to reach the barrier, and what does the patient do?
A: Apply traction; patient pulls the hip cephalad
C: Flex the hip further; patient pulls the knee toward the chest
D: Flex the hip further; patient pushes the knee into the shoulder (hip extension)
E: Extend the hip off the table; patient pushes the knee toward the ceiling
explanation: Anterior rotation ME: flex the hip and knee to rotate the innominate posteriorly to the barrier; the patient gently pushes the knee into the physician's shoulder (hip extension, hamstrings) for 3–5 s; relax and flex further; repeat 3–5 times. Reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 75.
reference: OPP 1 Study Guide Written Exam 3 (Fotopoulos), p. 75
